# Rats and Ravens

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

**Rats and Ravens** is an original 2D platformer for the **ClockworkPi PicoCalc**, by **Thomas
Dzubin**, written in C against the **Raspberry Pi Pico SDK** and the driver
layer from
[`picocalc-text-starter`](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter)
by **Blair Leduc** (LCD and south-bridge keyboard drivers) — vendored here
under [`picocalc-text-starter-main/`](picocalc-text-starter-main/). Also
runs on Windows and Linux via a bundled SDL2 desktop port. Not based on or
inspired by any specific existing game.

```
platformer.c                 the whole program
platformer_config.h          every #define / tunable constant
CMakeLists.txt                builds the firmware, reusing picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/*
desktop/                      Desktop (SDL2) build for Windows and Linux: CMakeLists.txt +
                              the small shim that stands in for the PicoCalc drivers
pico_sdk_import.cmake        standard Pico SDK locator (copied from the starter)
picocalc-text-starter-main/  vendored driver layer (see License; do not edit)
LICENSE, CHANGELOG.md        MIT licence; version history
```

## Where this stands

**Milestone 4: movement / jump / camera-scroll / scoring / randomly
generated levels.** Every level is randomly generated — its own
gaps, towers, platforms, foggy zones (ground-flush or floating),
pickups, and rat_ravens (a patrol hazard — see below) — instead of one
hand-placed layout, plus a score, a countdown timer, gold coin pickups, and a
win condition (see below). The player, rats, ravens, and pickups are
small sprites; still no real level *themes* yet — geometry is random,
content is not.

Every obstacle, the ground included, is fully solid: the character cannot
pass through any side of one — walking into a tower's side stops you, and
jumping into a platform's underside from below stops you there too. See
`SOLIDS[]` and `step_physics()` in `platformer.c`.

A one-line debug readout (position, vertical velocity, grounded state,
double-jump charges left, power-up seconds remaining) exists for tuning
the movement feel; off by default (`ENABLE_DEBUG_READOUT` in
`platformer_config.h`).

## Physics

Fixed-point (no float), fixed 16ms timestep. Position and velocity are
stored in subpixels; the main loop measures real elapsed time and runs
however many whole 16ms steps that covers, capped so a stall can't make
the game leap forward when it resumes. This keeps the feel identical on
RP2040 (no hardware FPU), RP2350, and the desktop build — see
`step_physics()` in `platformer.c`.

Every jump is a fixed, predictable height — there is no "hold to jump
higher." How high a jump goes depends only on which of three launch
velocities fired it: the ground jump (~99px), the weaker double jump, or
the jewel (~150px on its own). Every physics/timing/geometry
constant lives in `platformer_config.h`. The screen's top edge is also a
hard ceiling — nothing can send the character above it, however jumps get
combined.

**Double jump.** Pressing SPACE/UP again while airborne spends one of
`MAX_AIR_JUMPS` (currently 1) extra jumps, on a weaker `AIR_JUMP_VELOCITY`.
It refills the instant you land. Chained right at the peak of a ground
jump, it reaches ~141px — enough to clear every generated platform and
tower with comfortable room (see "Power-ups are always optional" below).

**Jewel.** At least two are placed per level (`MIN_JEWELS`),
somewhere reachable — on a tower, on a platform, floating in open air, or
inside a foggy zone. Touching one makes *every* jump — ground or air —
launch at the stronger `POWERUP_JUMP_VELOCITY` for `POWERUP_DURATION_MS`
(7.5 seconds): a genuine energy boost to the character, not a change to
gravity, so a single powered-up jump clears even the tallest generated
tower on its own. It also lets the character walk straight across a
ground gap instead of falling to a death, for as long as it stays active.
It wears off on its own; its countdown only runs while the game does, so
pausing doesn't use it up.

**Power-ups are always optional.** A core rule of this project: the
character must be able to progress with zero power-ups active — a
power-up only ever makes it *easier*, never required. Towers take this
further than most obstacles: a tower is a full-width solid wall with no
way around it, only over it, so EVERY generated tower (`TOWER_H_MIN`..
`TOWER_H_MAX`, 72-120px) must be clearable by a well-timed double jump
alone, not just *some* of them. The power-up still makes every tower
easier, just never the only way up.

**Visible state.** The character's fill colour is a minor cue: cyan while
a double jump is still "spent" for the current trip (resets on landing),
black while sick from a rat_raven (see Rat_ravens below). The jewel
doesn't recolour the character at all — it adds a white outline on top of
whatever the fill colour already is, noticeably thicker than sick's outline
(which stays thin, existing only so a solid-black sick body isn't
invisible, not as an eye-catching cue).

**Foggy zones.** Patches of thick cloud / dense branches, several per
level (some ground-flush, some floating; ground-flush ones start only 16px
tall on level 1 and grow to their full 48–88px random height by level 8) —
*not* solid: walking or
jumping straight into one works, but for as long as any part of the
character overlaps it, gravity is off and walking is slowed. UP (or
SPACE) queues a small, bounded climb (`FOGGY_STEP_PX`); DOWN queues the
same amount of descend; either is worked off gradually rather than fired
all at once, so each press reads as one slow, deliberate step — it takes
several UP presses in a row to climb clear of the zone, not one. With
nothing queued, the character holds position — but stand still (no keys
at all) inside a zone, or on top of one, for about 3 seconds and the
character starts to sink slowly, one pixel every few ticks; any key press
resets the wait and stops the sinking. **Fog levels** (every fourth level) add one extra ground zone spanning
the whole level, as tall as a ground zone can be. Clear
the top by climbing and the zone's top edge catches the character as a
landing ledge — grounded, with a real jump and the double jump both
refilled, same as landing on solid ground; from there, either jump away,
or press DOWN to step back down into the zone. Walk off the ledge
sideways and gravity resumes normally. A floating zone (clear air both
above and below it) works the same in reverse: descending past its
bottom edge resumes normal gravity and falls the rest of the way to the
ground. The power-up overrides all of it: a powered-up jump launches at
full strength, with normal gravity, even inside one. A foggy zone's
position is independent of every other obstacle — it's fine for one to
sit partly under a platform or tower; if a climb runs into that solid on
the way up, it's simply blocked there, same as a jump would be. A floating
zone that's too high to reach with a double jump directly from the ground
always has a platform nearby that the player could land on first and jump
from instead.

## Random levels & the camera

Every level is randomly generated (`generate_level()` in `platformer.c`):
its own gaps, towers,
platforms, foggy zones, and pickups. Obstacles and pickups live in world
coordinates, not screen coordinates. A horizontal-only camera follows the
character with a dead-zone: it can move freely in a band in the middle of
the screen before the camera starts scrolling to keep up, an instant snap
rather than a smoothed follow. The camera is clamped so it never shows
past either end of the level. Rendering only ever repaints what's
actually near the screen — a full viewport repaint when the camera itself
moves, or the usual small dirty-rectangle patch when it hasn't — so the
cost doesn't grow with how wide a level gets, only with how many
obstacles are actually near the visible screen.

Placement is retry-based: a candidate spot that would overlap something
it shouldn't is rejected and retried a bounded number of times, rather
than an exhaustive solvability proof. Solids (ground/towers/platforms)
never overlap each other; foggy zones and pickups only avoid overlapping
their own kind, purely so two overlapping icons or zone rectangles don't
draw as one indistinguishable blob — a foggy zone overlapping a solid is
fine and intentional. Reasonable constraints (gap widths within jump
range, a safe margin at both ends of the level so the start and the win
line always have solid ground) aim for levels that are almost always
fair, not a guarantee every one is completable. A few more keep every
level free of spots nothing can reach: every platform keeps at least a
player-height of clear space under it (so a tower top is never a
crawlspace), no pickup is ever placed inside a tower or platform, and no
rat_raven ever starts inside one.

Reaching the level's far right edge is a **win**: a "YOU WIN!" message
shows, and either a brand new level starts (any key) or the same level
starts over (ENTER) — see "Scoring, the timer, and gold coins" below. Either
way score resets to 0 along with everything else (timer, pickups,
position).

**Object sizes.** Every object's width and height is a multiple of 8
pixels, so on hardware that supports it, any of them could be filled with
an 8x8-tile texture instead of a flat colour — the player is 16x24, a rat_raven is 16x16, a pickup is 8x8, and towers/platforms/foggy zones are all
sized in multiples of 8 too. Positions aren't snapped to the grid, only
the sizes are.

## Scoring, the timer, and gold coins

Score comes from gold coin pickups (`COIN_VALUE`, 20 each), stomping a rat_raven (`STOMP_VALUE`, 25), and the time bonus on the win screen — moving
left or right doesn't affect it. A 2-minute countdown
(`TIMER_DURATION_MS`), shown as `MM:SS`, ticks down once per physics
step, so it pauses along with everything else. Reaching 0, or falling
into a gap, is a **death**: a "YOU DIED" message shows, with a one-line
reason underneath — "YOU RAN OUT OF TIME," "YOU FELL INTO A GAP," "A
RAT KILLED YOU" or "A RAVEN KILLED YOU" (a ground or a flying rat_raven) — and any key except Q retries the *same* level from the
beginning: score, timer, every pickup, and every rat_raven's position all
reset, but the layout doesn't change (only winning generates a new one).
The message line shows `PRESS Q TO QUIT` on this screen; Q goes back to
the splash screen on the PicoCalc and exits the program on the desktop.

Either way, the end screen enforces at least a 2-second pause — with the
keyboard buffer continuously drained the whole time, so a still-held or
mashed key can't skip straight past it — before it'll accept a fresh key
to continue.

A win instead shows the time *left* on the clock, in seconds (e.g. "TIME BONUS: 45s",
in smaller text than the score, erased once the countdown ends; the same seconds the `TIME:` status line was showing), then — after a
one-second pause — rapidly counts that number down to 0 while the score
counts up, 3 points per second (`TIME_BONUS_PER_SECOND`), with a beep every five seconds counted
off: a faster playing time leaves more time on the clock and so earns a
bigger bonus. After that, a `MISSED COINS: N` line counts down the same
way while the score drops by 5 for every gold coin pickup left uncollected
(`MISSED_COIN_PENALTY`; the score stops at 0). This is a real, permanent
bonus, not just a visual effect: whatever score the countdown ends at
is what gets compared against `LEVEL HIGH SCORE:` (see below) before
score resets to 0 for the next attempt — it never carries between
levels or retries.

**Gold coins** are a fixed-count pickup (`COIN_PER_LEVEL`, 30, per level,
regardless of how wide it is) worth `COIN_VALUE` (20) score each, drawn
gold/orange, gone once collected. It's never on the ground — always on a
platform or tower, floating in open air needing a jump, or inside a
foggy zone. The jewel (at least `MIN_JEWELS`, 2, per level;
drawn blue/cyan) and every gold coin pickup share one mechanism (`PICKUPS[]`):
it doesn't matter where a pickup is placed — open air, on a solid, or
inside a foggy zone — collecting it works the same way regardless.

Level, time, and score are shown bigger than the driver's normal text, in
two status lines near the top of the screen — `LEVEL:1 TIME:01:23` on
one, `SCORE:100` right below it. A third line, at normal text size, shows
`LEVEL HIGH SCORE:` and the best score this specific level layout has
ever been won with — it resets to 0 whenever a new level is generated,
so it's tracking your best result on the level you're currently playing,
not a lifetime total. A fourth line, same size, shows a short hint:
`ARROWS TO MOVE.  SPACE TO JUMP` on level 1, `WATCH OUT FOR THE RATS AND RAVENS`
on level 2, and `THE FOG IS THICK` on fog levels (which take priority over
the level 1 and 2 hints). While something is going on, a state message
replaces the hint, most urgent first: `YOU FEEL SICK` while sick, then
`YOU FEEL GREAT!` while a jewel is active, then `YOU ARE IN THICK
FOG` while inside a foggy zone; when none applies the hint returns. All
messages use the gold coin pickup's gold colour.

Above level 20, rat_ravens get 5% faster per level, up to double speed
at level 40 and beyond (`RAT_RAVEN_SPEED_RAMP_*` in `platformer_config.h`).

Rat_ravens are drawn as a rat (ground) and a raven (flying), 16x16 pictures
from `rat_raven_sprites.h`; the collision box is unchanged. Set
`RAT_RAVEN_USE_SPRITES` to 0 in `platformer_config.h` to go back to the
plain squares.

The solids have surface detail: grass and darker soil on the ground, stone
towers with mortar lines, windows and a notched cap, wooden platforms with
plank gaps, and light / dark bevel edges (`SOLID_TEXTURES` in
`platformer_config.h` turns it off).

Foggy zones stay still on levels 1 to 9. From level 10 on (`FOG_DRIFT_START_LEVEL`)
they drift slowly left and right, at half the ground rat_raven's speed,
reversing at the level's edges or when they would touch another foggy zone;
the level-wide fog layer does not move. A drifting zone also carries the
player sideways while they are inside it or standing on top of it (not while
they stand on real ground), and a wall stops a carried player; once the
fog has moved on, the player drops. You can still walk around inside it.
A coin or jewel placed inside a drifting zone drifts along with it, so it
is never left stranded in mid-air out of reach. The fog is textured with
soft lighter and darker streaks (`FOG_TEXTURE`).

Special levels: every 7th level has twice the gold coin pickups (`LOTS TO
COLLECT`), every 9th twice the jewels (`LOTS OF JEWELS`), every
13th twice the rat_ravens (`MANY RATS AND RAVENS`), and level 10 has no rat_ravens
and no gaps (`NOTHING BAD ON 10`). Where they coincide, all the effects
apply but the message follows that order: level 10, then 13, 9, 7, fog.

On the win screen, pressing ENTER instead of any other key replays the
SAME level layout again from the start (instead of moving on to a new
one) so you can try to beat that high score; any other key moves on to
a new level as usual, the way it always has.

## Rat_ravens

*(These are called "rat_ravens" in the code and in this document. Thomas
may call them "spiders" or "ghosts" in conversation — they're the same
thing; they just don't look like either.)*

A patrol hazard, in two kinds. **Ground** rat_ravens (drawn as rats)
patrol the ground at `RAT_RAVEN_SPEED`, the same block size as the
player. Reverses direction when it walks into a tower or
reaches either end of the level, and also when it reaches the edge of a
gap: a ground rat_raven never crosses a gap. **Flying** rat_ravens (drawn
as ravens) behave the same way, except they
patrol 110 to 220 pixels above the ground instead of on it — the same
height on the PicoCalc and the desktop build — bobbing
up or down, at random, by half their own height every half second, never
leaving those limits, at twice the speed, and reverse off a platform as well as a
tower (nothing to jump over up there, so gaps don't matter to them at
all). Either kind never spawns close enough to the player's own start
position to hit before you've had a chance to react, and either kind's
speed is halved for as long as it's inside a foggy zone.

Rat_raven count scales with the level number, not level width: levels 1-2
spawn 6 rat_ravens, levels 3-4 spawn 12, levels 5-6 spawn 24, levels 7-8
and up spawn 40, a hard cap. About 1 in 4 of them is flying, but every level is
guaranteed at least one flying rat_raven no matter how that chance happens
to land. Dying and retrying the same level doesn't change the level
number, the rat_raven count, or which ones are flying; only winning (a
brand new, harder level) does.

Touching one while normal makes the character **sick**: it turns black,
outlined in white the same way as rat_ravens, then slowly fades back up to
its normal colour over the sickness time so you can see it recovering,
until either a jewel
pickup cures it instantly (gold coins do not — only jewels do), or it
survives 30 seconds on its own — back to **well** (plain green), needing
two fresh rat_raven hits before the next death. Touching a (different) rat_raven while already sick is that second hit: a death — but staying in
contact with the very same rat_raven for a couple of extra ticks right
after the first hit doesn't count as a separate touch; a brief grace
period requires genuinely breaking contact first. If the jewel
is active at the moment of a hit, it shields the character instead: no
sickness, but the power-up itself ends immediately (back to a plain green
block, no outline).

Every one of those three outcomes uses up the rat_raven that caused it,
removing it from the level, same as dropping onto one from above — off a
ledge, or on the way down out of a jump — which stomps it instead and
leaves the player completely untouched. Rat_ravens come back if you die
and retry the same level, same as everything else.

## Sound

On the win screen, once the time bonus has been added and the final score
is showing, a short happy song (under 5 seconds) plays.

A cheerful two-tone jingle plays on a gold coin pickup, and a quick rising
three-tone one on a jewel; a
single lower-pitched tone plays when a rat_raven makes the character sick,
and again whenever the run ends in death, whatever the cause. A stomp-kill,
and the shield outcome (surviving a rat_raven hit thanks to an active jewel
power-up), play a sharp high-to-low "pow" sound instead — sickness and
death keep the sad tone as the main audio cue rather than layering the
impact sound on top of it. Winning explicitly silences whatever sound was
still playing at that exact moment, so a pickup jingle or rat_raven tone
never bleeds into the win sequence. All of this plays through the
PicoCalc's stereo PWM audio, and identically on the Windows/Linux desktop
build through a real SDL2 audio backend (`desktop/shim_audio.c`) — no
separate silent stub.

## Controls

| Key                    | Action                                      |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| LEFT / RIGHT            | move (full speed while held; no acceleration or friction yet) |
| SPACE or UP             | jump. Press again in mid-air for one more, weaker jump (double jump). Inside a foggy zone: a small step up instead. |
| DOWN                    | (foggy zones only, including while standing on top of one) a small step down |
| ENTER or P               | pause / resume -- shows/hides a "PAUSED" message on screen. Everything stops: timers, the jewel, and any sound effect that was playing |
| ESC                     | firmware: quit to the splash screen, no confirmation. Desktop: confirms first, then exits the program |
| Q                       | firmware: quit to the splash screen, asks to confirm first. Desktop: confirms, then exits the program the same way ESC does |
| L                       | choose a level: type one or two digits (ENTER after a single digit, ESC to cancel) and the game restarts at that level |
| A / S / D / F           | left / up / down / right, the same as the arrow keys, so the game is easier to play on a laptop keyboard. Not shown on any in-game help screen. |
| ~ (SHIFT + `)           | reboot into BOOTSEL (USB drive) mode          |

On the win screen only, ENTER means "retry this level" instead of pause;
see "Scoring, the timer, and gold coins" above.

## Building

VS Code Pico extension (Compile / Run), or from a terminal with
`PICO_SDK_PATH` set:

```
cmake -B build -G Ninja
ninja -C build
```

Output: `build/picocalc-platformer-<chip>.uf2` (`<chip>` is `RP2350` or
`RP2040`, matching the board), which the build also copies to the
top-level folder as `picocalc-platformer-RP2350.uf2` or
`picocalc-platformer-RP2040.uf2`, so both chips' builds can sit side by
side. Flash by copying to the `RPI-RP2` drive — hold BOOTSEL on power-up,
or press `~` (SHIFT + backtick) in the app.

### Windows

The same program runs on Windows through a small SDL2 layer in
[`desktop/`](desktop/) that stands in for the PicoCalc's LCD, keyboard,
and audio. The desktop build's game area is bigger than the PicoCalc's —
640x480 instead of 320x320 — so there's more of the level visible at
once, on a full PC keyboard. From an MSYS2 UCRT64 shell with SDL2
installed:

```
cmake -S desktop -B build-windows -G Ninja
ninja -C build-windows
```

Output: `picocalc-platformer-Windows.exe` in the top-level folder (its
window is titled "Rats and Ravens"). SDL2 is
linked statically, so it is a single file with no `SDL2.dll`. The keys are
the same as the table above (`~` simply closes the program).

### Linux

The same source builds on Linux with the SDL2 development package installed
(for example `sudo apt install libsdl2-dev`). Unlike the Windows build, SDL2
is **not** linked in statically: the program links `libSDL2` dynamically,
and the build copies that library next to the executable as
`libSDL2-2.0.so.0`, where the executable finds it through an `$ORIGIN`
run-path. Keep the two files together.

    cmake -S desktop -B build-linux
    cmake --build build-linux

Output: `picocalc-platformer-Linux` and `libSDL2-2.0.so.0` in the top-level
folder.

## Status

Actively developed. Every mechanic described above — movement, jumping,
collision, camera scroll, foggy zones, scoring, the timer, gold coins, rat_ravens, sound, and random level generation — has been playtested on real
RP2350 hardware and confirmed working, including a 10-person playtest
session. The Windows desktop port has also been built and tested, at its
own larger 640x480 size with independent sound. No known open bugs as of
the latest playtest. See `CHANGELOG.md` for the detailed, dated history
of what changed and why.
